title: CBT@EmTech - CardioVascular Biomechanics Training Program at Emory and GaTech
text: This interdisciplinary Program in Cardiovascular Biomechanics at Emory University and Georgia Tech (CBT@EmTech) will train the next generation of biomedical engineers to study how biomechanics affects cardiovascular diseases. Trainees will receive formal coursework, research training, and professional development that will enable them to apply an integration of engineering, vascular biology, data sciences, and biosciences to unsolved problems in cardiovascular medicine. We expect these trainees to be thought leaders in the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular disease.

title: Homeostatic Mechanisms Regulating Mitochondrial Health
text:
(Public health relevance statement)
Mitochondria are indispensable organelles that generate energy and perform other vital functions for
eukaryotic cells. Human health therefore depends on the proper function of mitochondria, and we are
studying the processes that maintain mitochondrial function in cells. In the long-term, advances from these
studies can be used to improve mitochondrial function and mitigate disease.

title: T32 Training Program in Pediatric Immuno-Oncology and Immunotherapy
text:
Immunotherapy is a promising treatment for pediatric cancer that can improve outcomes while minimizing toxicity
and the long-term adverse effects associated with other types of therapy. The success of this treatment requires
more discovery-based researchers who aim to improve understanding of how pediatric cancer cells interact with
the immune system, and translational researchers to refine immunotherapeutic approaches for use in early
phase clinical studies. The Pediatric Immuno-Oncology and Immunotherapy training program is designed to
provide integrated training in advanced research approaches in a clinical context to foster the development of
the next generation of independent scientists leading the field.

title: Designing Personalized Formulations with Machine Learning
text:
Drug formulations are key to enable the safe and effective delivery of therapeutics but are currently costly to
produce or insufficiently optimized for specific drugs and specific patients. We will here develop novel platforms
that tightly integrate machine learning and experiments to more rapidly and effectively design (1) functional
excipients, (2) targeted nanoparticles, and (3) prodrugs. Our research will pioneer and prototype innovative
approaches in the nascent field of computational drug delivery and will also produce targeted drug formulations
that provide safer and more effective therapies for every patient.

title: Neurobehavioral Effects of Frequent Co-use of Alcohol and Cannabis
text:
Individuals who use alcohol and marijuana simultaneously are at increased risk for developing substance use
disorders. The proposed project aims to understand how simultaneous use leads to increased risk for negative
outcomes by examining the brain’s response to stress cues, neuroendocrine responses to stress cues, and
relationships between stress, craving, and drug use in the real world. By elucidating brain and behavioral
mechanisms, it may be possible to identify treatments to prevent or reduce the negative consequences of
simultaneous use.

title: GABA signaling in the nTS and cardiorespiratory responses to hypoxia
text:
Many cardiorespiratory diseases manifest as unstable breathing and episodic periods of hypoxia resulting in
sympathetic-mediated hypertension; an exaggerated chemoreflex and its brain interaction are implicated in these
responses. Our studies will determine the importance of altered GABA-mediated inhibition in sensory and
brainstem reflex neurons in an episodic hypoxia rat model. We expect to define how targeting these brain
mechanisms can be used to design rational and novel therapeutic approaches to the consequences of hypoxia.

title: Quantitative MRI and Deep Learning Technologies for Classification of NAFLD
text:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), including elastography (MRE), is a promising technology for the non-
invasive assessment of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), but still cannot reliably distinguish simple
steatosis from non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) - the severe form of NAFLD that can lead to fibrosis,
cirrhosis, and even death. This project will develop a new suite of rapid and robust free-breathing quantitative
MRI techniques in combination with multi-parametric deep learning models to accurately classify simple
steatosis versus NASH and measure the degree of fibrosis. The new MRI and deep learning technologies will
be validated and tested in patients with NAFLD, ranging from simple steatosis to NASH, to characterize the
classification performance and establish a framework that can be used in the future to improve management of
patients with NAFLD.

title: Preserving chromatin nano-structure to enhance chondrocyte therapeutic potential for cartilage repair
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it may enhance the therapeutic potential of
chondrocytes for repairing early stage cartilage injuries and preventing degeneration of the joint, which is an
unmet clinical need. The project is relevant to NIH's mission as it will open new horizons for studying how in vitro
expansion and chemo-physical cues regulate chromatin organization resulting in the loss or preservation of
phenotype, which will be applicable to multiple cell-based therapies.

title: 1/11 Integrative Neuroscience Initiative on Alcoholism
text:
INIA-Neuroimmune is a multi-disciplinary, highly collaborative research consortium that studies immune and
inflammatory pathways in the brain, combining novel genomic and systems-level analyses to identify potential
treatments for alcohol use disorder. The closely integrated approach using multiple levels of evaluation, from
computational to behavioral, will provide key information about genes and biological pathways that contribute
to excessive drinking and will identify candidate drug targets for developing new treatments.

title: Human Ocular Surface Electrophysiology
text:
Dry eye disease is a multifactorial disease of the ocular surface characterized by impaired tear film
homeostasis accompanied by ocular symptoms that affects approximately 6.8% of adults in the USA, with a
global prevalence as high as 50%. Despite this significant disease burden, there are currently just four FDA-
approved therapies for dry eye disease, each targeting only the inflammatory pathway and having limited
efficacy. The proposed research will advance novel dry eye disease therapeutics that promote tear fluid
secretion by targeting ion transport proteins on epithelial cells lining the ocular surface.

title: The evolution and genetics of recombination rate variation
text:
The amount of genetic shuffling due to meiotic recombination each generation (i.e., recombination rate) has
profound effects on patterns of inheritance and is a key modulator of evolutionary processes such as
adaptation and speciation. Despite its wide-ranging importance across many domains of biology, we have a
poor understanding of how and why recombination rate varies across biological scales. To address this gap,
my lab will shed light on the genetic and evolutionary causes and consequences of recombination rate
variation in natural populations by testing long-standing hypotheses using modern genomic tools.

title: Core C - Genomics, CRISPR, and Gene Perturbation Core
text:
Autoimmunity, cancer and chronic infections are significant causes of morbidity and mortality. T cells are
central to these diseases and their activities are regulated by the cell surface inhibitory receptors PD1 and
LAG3. This Core will provide services to use genomic sequencing, CRISPR and computational approaches to
define the role of the inhibitory receptors PD1 and LAG3 in autoimmunity, cancer and chronic infections.

title: Cannabis use following trauma exposure: An observational study of the impact of acute stress and fear response on cannabis outcomes
text:
The impact of cannabis use (CU) on public health has become an increasingly pressing concern, particularly
among emerging adults, who evidence tremendous plasticity in neurophysiological functioning but are at
increased risk for both elevated rates of CU and trauma exposure. Little is known about how acute
posttraumatic stress symptoms, as well as alterations in fear response and physiology, impact cannabis use
behavior, especially during the days and weeks immediately following trauma exposure. The present
investigation examines in vivo momentary and biological processes implicated in the development of negative
outcomes of trauma including cannabis misuse and posttraumatic stress disorder among emerging adults
during the acute posttrauma period.

title: Methodology Core
text: METHODOLOGY CORE ABSTRACT The Methodology Core is central to our CCCR's goal of acting as a hub and resource for conducting and disseminating high quality clinical research in rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases (RMD). This Core brings together investigators from diverse scientific backgrounds whose clinical research expertise will serve the broader RMD research community in the following ways: 1) Provide support in advanced epidemiologic methods, statistical approaches, and machine learning approaches; 2) Utilize and make available our CCCR's cohort studies and large administrative claims and electronic health records databases; 3) Advise on outcome measures and provide training in specialized study protocols (e.g., quantitative sensory testing, imaging, wearable sensors); 4) Provide input regarding conditions for which we have unique expertise, including osteoarthritis, crystal-related arthritis, spondyloarthritis, and musculoskeletal pain mechanisms, though the methods expertise and resources allow for broad application to the study of other RMDs. In this renewal, we will expand our use of, and guidance related to, advanced causal inference, machine learning and deep learning, and digital health applications (including wearable sensors). A new area we will add in the renewal is implementation science to enhance our capabilities to narrow the knowledge-practice gap and health inequities in key RMDs. A key feature of this Core is a weekly clinical research meeting, known as the Research Accelerator, in which a diverse group of researchers provide interdisciplinary input into all facets of clinical research projects. By having rheumatology, rehabilitation, epidemiology, biostatistics, and other specialized investigators meet once a week together, the Methodology Core creates interdisciplinary conversations and makes available methodologic expertise to clinician researchers that would otherwise not be part of their grants or scientific projects. Our Boston University CCCR group is well known for training early-stage investigators, many of whom are prominent clinical researchers in RMD research domestically and globally. The Methodology Core will continue to emphasize training. In this renewal, we will expand our educational programming, including a new Visiting Professor program, an expanded monthly journal club with virtual attendance options for the broader research community, an Advanced Methodology Seminar to act as a continuing education opportunity for our analysts and methodologists, and will leverage social media to provide summary “threads” from our various educational sessions and to showcase our CCCR work. Through these endeavors, the Core will expand and enrich the scope of research questions addressed and methods used to address them, ultimately benefiting the health and quality of life of individuals living with RMDs.

title: Recreating Human Developmental Hematopoietic Niches for Ex Vivo Biomanufacturing of Blood Stem Cells
text:
We are reconstructing the early human tissues that give rise to blood and immune cells to gain a
deeper understanding of how these vital cells develop. By combining stem cell biology with AI-
driven modeling, we aim to recreate these environments and cultivate healthy blood stem cells
for therapeutic use, including disease treatment and recovery after bone marrow transplants. Our
work could lead to a novel platform for regenerative medicine, making stem cell therapies more
reliable, accessible, and effective for patients across all ages.

title: Biochemistry of Pre-mRNA Splicing
text:
RNA splicing is a fundamental step in normal gene expression, involving the precise removal of non-coding
segments during the maturation of messenger RNA. Abnormal RNA splicing due to mutations in gene sequences
that control the process, or to alterations in the splicing machinery, gives rise to a wide variety of diseases. By
studying the fundamental mechanisms responsible for RNA-splicing specificity, and ways in which this process
can be manipulated, the proposed research will facilitate the correct classification of mutations that affect
splicing, and the design of more effective RNA-targeted therapeutics.

title: Evolution and Engineering of Specificity in Antimicrobial Peptides
text:
Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) form the first line of defense against opportunistic bacterial infections, and
they hold promise as potential therapeutic compounds. Whereas AMPs were previously believed to have
broad-spectrum antibiotic activity, new evidence suggests the potential for high degrees of specificity. This
project combines functional and evolutionary genetics to understand how natural AMPs target specific
pathogens and evolve in response to environmental microbes, then integrates that information to engineer
novel AMPs with desired antimicrobial activity.

title: The function of LIN28B and follistatin in supporting cell reprogramming and hair cell regeneration in the murine cochlea
text:
Mechano-sensory hair cells within our ear are essential for our ability to detect sound. Hair cells are not
regenerated and their loss is a leading cause for deafness in humans.
In our proposal, we will investigate whether re-activation of the progenitor-specific genes Lin28b and follistatin
will enable supporting cells to re-activate a progenitor-like state and allow them to regenerate lost hair cells.
We anticipate that insights gained from our study will provide exiting new avenues for cell-based hearing
restoration efforts.

title: Sequencing and sample core: genetic errors of immunity
text: Project Summary—Core A The exponential growth of next-generation sequencing has revolutionized the study of genetic errors of immunity. We, as a community, have collectively identified over 500 genetic lesions leading to immune dysregulation syndromes. These syndromes encompass susceptibility to infections, autoinflammation, autoimmunity, allergy and cancer. The identification and characterization of genetic lesions is paving the way for the use of personalized medicine and the study of rare genetic syndromes. Despite the tremendous success achieved, the genetic cause of the disease remains to be identified in over 70% of families. Furthermore, even when a genetic lesion is identified, it may not segregate perfectly with the disease. Thus, some individuals carrying the mutation are very ill, whereas others display little or no clinical disease (low clinical penetrance of the disease). Both of these problems — the absence of a known genetic cause of disease and variable disease penetrance — require further investigation. We now have opportunities to study samples from human subjects with an unprecedented degree of granularity, and advances in next-generation sequencing are making it possible to decipher increasingly complex datasets for genetic and molecular signatures. These samples were obtained from human subjects with unknown genetic lesions or known genetic lesions, from families in which clinical disease has incomplete penetrance. The human sequencing and sample core will streamline the datasets available for all enrolled patients and their families, by storing samples, sequencing (DNA and RNA) in bulk and at single-cell levels at typical and extraordinary depths, and will store the sequencing results, sharing these data with the bioinformatics core and associated projects. By reducing barriers and uniformizing data from different sources in our shared approaches it should be possible to increase the efficiency of data collection and downstream analyses for all P01 projects.

title: Alcohol Stimulation and Sedation in Binge Drinkers
text:
Understanding the factors contributing to development and persistence of excessive alcohol consumption is
crucial for improved prevention, education, and intervention strategies. The Chicago Social Drinking Project
uniquely integrates human laboratory alcohol challenge, high-resolution ecological momentary assessment of
real-world drinking, and longitudinal assessment of drinking behaviors and symptoms of alcohol use disorder in
people across the lifespan. The approach will provide critical tests of the prospective role of stimulating,
rewarding, sedating, and negative affect reducing effects of alcohol to the vulnerability, severity, and
maintenance of excessive drinking and alcohol use disorder.
